concept: High-leverage short trading and risk of ruin
summary: Evidence status: research claims ungated (v4 evidence gate not passed); treat as leads with cited sources. Educational, not financial advice; leverage can lose more than the stake. A high-leverage short (a perpetual-futures short or a borrow-and-sell equity short) is a position whose liquidation price sits close to entry, so a squeeze, funding drain or gap can force closure before a stop fills; the pack collects 143 cited units from 62 sources on liquidation-price formulas, borrow versus perp mechanics, funding carry, stop placement against the liquidation buffer, and sizing by Kelly, fixed fractional and volatility targeting, with risk-of-ruin limits.

facts.text: US equity short margin is a fixed multiple of position value. Regulation T requires 150 percent of the current market value for a short sale of a non-exempt security (100 percent where a security exchangeable or convertible within 90 days is held, subject to conditions). FINRA Rule 4210 maintenance margin for a short stock priced at $5.00 or more is the greater of $5.00 per share or 30 percent of current market value; below $5.00 it is the greater of $2.50 per share or 100 percent.

Funding is a transfer between traders, not an exchange fee. Binance says it charges no fee on funding payments and that they move directly between holders of opposing positions. Hyperliquid says funding is purely peer-to-peer and collects no fee on the payments.

A volatility-based stop for a short is the Chandelier Exit: n-day lowest low plus ATR(n) x multiplier, with defaults of n = 22 and multiplier 3.0 (StockCharts, Corporate Finance Institute). CFI says stops widen in high-volatility sessions and tighten in low-volatility ones; StockCharts says volatile instruments may need a higher multiplier. Both attribute the indicator to Chuck Le Beau.

KuCoin's published short examples need care. (a) Its USDT-margined isolated formula returns a price below entry for a short (29,265.4, using the inputs of its own long example with side = −1) unless position size and opening value are entered as negative numbers; the negative-sign convention is stated in its cross-margin section, not beside the isolated formula. (b) Its coin-margined formula as printed ('1 − side × MMR − side × LFR', short side = −1) gives 33,586.7 for its own short example, but the worked example uses (1 − 0.7% − 0.06%) and rounded values (0.033 and 0.0033) to reach 33,414; e

facts.text: Cascades create bad debt even on venues built to prevent it. Chitra's abstract: on 2025-10-10 Hyperliquid used autodeleveraging 'repeatedly to close $2.1 billion of positions in 12 minutes'. Sepper (2026-03-10) reports that '$2.1 billion in liquidations over 12 minutes generated $304.5 million in deficits requiring socialization', and defines bad debt as arising 'when execution price is worse than bankruptcy price', meaning liquidation fills below the price at which equity hit zero. This is the venue-level form of loss beyond margin. Sepper takes the figure from Chitra et al., so the two sourc

Drawdown odds in the continuous model (r = 0, no jumps, instant rebalancing): full Kelly doubles before halving with probability 2/3; half Kelly with probability 8/9 while keeping 3/4 of the growth rate. The probability of ever falling to a fraction x of starting capital is x^(2/c - 1) when betting c x Kelly (Thorp Eq. 7.13), so the chance of ever losing half of capital is 1/2 at full Kelly and 1/8 at half Kelly. MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba Table 3 gives matching values (0.67 and 0.89 for doubling before halving, relative growth 0.75 at half Kelly).

Fixed fractional is the same family as fractional Kelly: for an i.i.d. process with a myopic policy (log or negative-power utility) the optimum is fixed-fraction betting, 'hence fractional Kelly includes all these policies' (MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba). With fraction 0 < f < 1 wealth never reaches exactly zero, so Thorp redefines ruin as P(X_n <= eps) tending to 1, which still happens when growth is negative; with a minimum bet size ruin in the standard sense is always possible but 'negligible' if the minimum is small relative to capital. Equal numbers of wins and losses at fraction f leave W_2

A perpetual-futures short is a derivative position, not a loan of the asset. A long and a short counterparty agree a price without exchanging anything except margin posted with the venue; no underlying has to be acquired, so there is nothing to borrow or deliver; and the contract never expires. Because nothing forces convergence at maturity, a funding payment from one side to the other (peer-to-peer; Hyperliquid collects no fee on it) is the mechanism that pulls the perp price toward spot.

Volatility targeting is procyclical. ECB (May 2020): volatility targets allow higher leverage in calm markets, fund managers 'have to liquidate leveraged positions when market volatility and cross-asset correlations surge', and 'a common feature of these strategies is the procyclical way in which leverage and volatility are linked'. Harvey et al. describe the same behaviour as momentum-like (positions are cut when volatility rises after negative returns); Moreira and Muir's strategy 'cashed out almost completely' in the fall of 2008.

In isolated mode the liquidation price moves linearly with the margin allocated. In the closed form, each extra unit of margin moves a short's liquidation price up by 1/(q × (1 + MMR)). In Bybit's first-order form, the 'Extra Margin Added / Contract Quantity' term moves it by 1/q. Hyperliquid notes that an isolated position's liquidation price depends on its leverage setting, because the margin allocated depends on the initial margin, while a cross position's does not.

The protective stop has to sit on the safe side of the liquidation price. IG: 'Set a stop-loss before your liquidation price.' Wealthsimple: 'Placing a stop-loss before your liquidation price lets you leave the trade on your own terms', and it should be set when the trade is opened. Hyperliquid: because the maintenance margin is not returned in a backstop liquidation, 'traders can place stop loss orders or exit the positions before the mark price reaches the liquidation price'. For a short the ordering is entry < stop < liquidation price (derived from the sources, not quoted).

A good Sharpe ratio does not make leverage safe. Peters: 'The Sharpe ratio is insensitive to leverage', because leverage scales return and volatility together, while time-average growth is not insensitive: it rises, peaks and then falls (see the growth-curve claim). A strategy with a high Sharpe ratio can still be over-levered into negative growth.

A mark-price trigger decides when the stop fires, not where it fills. Binance says a stop-market order 'will be filled at the next available market price' and that with Mark Price triggers the execution price 'may deviate further from your trigger price'. Hyperliquid's FAQ says 'TP/SL are triggered by mark price, and then executed' and that 'Trade price and mark price are different'.

'No borrow cost' holds for order-book perps but not for pool-based perps. GMX's synthetics README says 'There is a borrowing fee paid to liquidity providers', sets borrowing factors separately for longs and shorts, and drives the rate by reserved USD relative to pool USD (curve model) or a usage factor (kink model); funding is paid separately, by the side with larger open interest. Gate Learn's summary likewise says traders pay borrowing fees because perps use pool capital, adjusted dynamically with capital utilization.

A stop set inside normal short-term price noise can be triggered and fill badly. SEC staff: a stop 'may be triggered by a short-term, intraday price move that results in an execution price for the stop order that is substantially worse', and brokers differ on whether last-sale or quotation prices trigger it. Hyperliquid builds its mark price from 'external CEX prices with Hyperliquid's book state', which it says is 'more robust than using a single instantaneous book price'.

freqtrade is an open-source reference implementation of per-exchange liquidation formulas. Its Binance function uses the transcribed Binance formula with a tier rate and maintenance amount; its Bybit function uses the first-order form and refuses inverse contracts. Its documentation says it 'is able to calculate liquidation prices, but does not calculate liquidation fees', so liquidations 'will result in inaccurate profit/loss results for your bot', and cross-margin interactions may not be fully simulated. In backtests the Binance function falls back to each other trade's open rate where live

The US 'must borrow first' gate is a locate, not a completed borrow. Rule 203(b)(1) of Regulation SHO bars a broker-dealer from accepting or effecting a short sale unless it has borrowed the security, has a bona-fide arrangement to borrow it, or has reasonable grounds to believe it can be borrowed for delivery when due, and it must document that compliance before the sale. Short sales by a market maker in bona-fide market making are excepted from the locate.

The room between stop and liquidation must cover the gap and slippage between trigger and fill. Mudrex: 'Placing your trigger too close to your liquidation price leaves almost no room for slippage'; its example has a stop at 95 above a liquidation price of 90, but price jumps from 97 to 91, so the stop fires too late. SEC staff say a triggered stop's fill can deviate significantly from the stop price, and Binance says a stop-market order fills at the next available market price.

Stops cluster at predictable levels and can cascade (FX evidence, not crypto). NY Fed Staff Report 150 (June 2002) reports that executed stop-loss sell orders cluster just below round numbers and stop-loss buy orders just above, that exchange-rate trends are 'unusually rapid' at levels where stops are documented to cluster, and that the response to stop-loss orders is larger and longer-lasting than to take-profit orders. Tentative extension: a short's buy-stop parked just above a round number or obvious high sits in a crowded trigger zone.

Kelly leverage assumes continuous rebalancing, which gaps break. Thorp: the optimal policy must adjust 'instantaneously'; in the October 1987 crash the S&P 500 fell 23% in one day, which would lift a 2.0x levered portfolio to 2.85x before it could be readjusted. He calls the 6.22x Kelly leverage in his Berkshire example inadvisable because prices 'may change suddenly and discontinuously'. Gerlach et al. (ETH Zurich simulation preprint, 2020): with the invested fraction restricted to [0, 1] Kelly 'never risks ruin even with jumps', but leverage or shorting makes negative wealth or bankruptcy po

Thorp's multi-asset Kelly model puts holding costs into the drift: if the rate paid on short-sale proceeds is r - e_s, the drift falls by e_s times the short fraction; if the borrowing rate is r + e_b, it falls by e_b times (long fraction - 1) for long exposure above 100%. An initial margin requirement q caps gross exposure at the sum of |f_i| <= 1/q. In his S&P 500 example (m = 0.11, s = 0.15, r = 0.06) the unconstrained Kelly leverage is 2.22; with a borrowing rate of r + 2% it falls to 1.33.

Hard leverage caps complement any sizing rule. Gerlach et al. cap the Kelly fraction at [-1, 2] and say their results demonstrate 'the importance of employing a limited leverage approach'; Moreira and Muir show that capping the volatility-managed weight at 1.5x kept the Sharpe ratio; Thorp's Berkshire example uses 2.0x, which he says was the maximum initial leverage allowed to customers by regulation at the time, and calls 6.22x inadvisable.

Computed here (a model result, not a sourced finding): the chance that a short at leverage L is liquidated within a horizon, with price as driftless geometric Brownian motion at 60% annual volatility, no maintenance margin and no fees. The barrier is a price rise of 1/L. First-passage formula: P = 1 - Phi((b - nu T)/(s sqrt(T))) + exp(2 nu b / s^2) Phi((-b - nu T)/(s sqrt(T))), with b = ln(1 + 1/L), nu = -s^2/2. Squeeze mechanics (the buy-side reading is an inference from the docs): when a short falls below maintenance margin, the venue closes it by buying. Hyperliquid first sends market orders for the full position to the book. For positions above 100k USDC it sends 20% at a time, with a 30-second cooldown after a partial liquidation. Below 2/3 of maintenance margin the position goes to the liquidator vault (HLP). Forced covering is price-insensitive demand, and depth is non-linear: FTI reports BTC top-of-book depth fell more than 90% on key venues during the 2025-10-10 sell-off, so the same flow mov

Volatility targeting levers up sharply in calm markets. Moreira and Muir's inverse-variance market weights have a median of 0.93 but 90th and 99th percentiles of 2.64x and 6.39x; scaling by realized volatility instead cuts the 99th percentile to 3.36x. Cederburg et al. report medians near 1 but 99th-percentile required leverage above 400% for every factor tested and up to 864% for momentum. Capping the weight at 1.5x kept the market Sharpe ratio at 0.53 (0.52 uncapped) but cut alpha from 4.86% to 3.10%.

The largest recorded crypto leverage wipe-out shows the scale. FTI Consulting (2025-12-24): on 2025-10-10 'more than $19 billion of crypto leverage was liquidated in roughly a day', top-of-book depth on key venues fell by more than 90%, and exchanges 'can forcibly liquidate positions before owners can react'. Bitcoin.com News: about 1.6 million traders were hit, about $16.7 billion of it long positions, perpetual open interest fell 43% ($217 billion to $123 billion), market makers estimated the true total at $30-40 billion, more than $150 billion was liquidated across 2025, and further events

Margin accounts add a ruin barrier that the standard growth model lacks. Peters: 'In geometric Brownian motion bankruptcy is impossible.' A real leveraged position is closed once an adverse move of about 1/L has used up its margin, less maintenance margin and fees. Binance Academy: with 5x leverage a $1,000 position needs $200 of collateral, a 20% buffer. ESMA's 2018 CFD limits run from 30:1 (a 3.3% move exhausts the margin) to 2:1 (50%), and its close-out rule acts at 50% of minimum required margin, earlier still. For a short the adverse move is a price rise.

Leverage ceilings differ by orders of magnitude between the two shorts. An equity borrow-and-sell short needs at least 30 percent of position value at maintenance under FINRA 4210 (150 percent initial under Regulation T), whereas Hyperliquid sets max leverage per perp asset between 3x and 40x and maintenance margin at half the initial margin at max leverage, i.e. 1.25 percent to 16.7 percent of position value. Other perp venues use their own tiers; none were read.

For coin-margined (inverse) contracts, a short's liquidation price is nonlinear in leverage. KuCoin's isolated formula puts position size in the numerator: LP = Q × (1 − m) / (OV − PM), where Q is the number of contracts, OV = Q / E is the opening value in coin, PM = OV / L is the position margin and m = MMR + liquidation fee rate. For a short this equals E × (1 − m) / (1 − 1/L), which tends to infinity as L approaches 1: a coin-margined short at 1× has no finite liquidation price, because its loss in coin is bounded by its margin. A linear short at 1× liquidates near 2E. At 2× with m = 0.76%

Binance funding caps: for listed symbols such as BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT and BNBUSDT, cap and floor are +/-0.75 x the maintenance margin ratio at maximum leverage. For other USDS-margined perpetuals the cap is a fixed +/-2%. Binance reserves the right to change cap and floor in extreme volatility. Single venue page.

Hyperliquid sets maintenance margin to half of the initial margin at an asset's maximum leverage: 1.25% for 40× assets up to 16.7% for 3× assets. With m = 1/(2 × Lmax), a short at maximum leverage is liquidated after an adverse move of 1/(2 × Lmax + 1) of entry: about 1.23% at 40× and 14.3% at 3× (computed from the closed form). A long at the same settings has 1/(2 × Lmax − 1): 1.27% at 40× and 20% at 3×. At maximum leverage, a trader can lose only about half of the initial margin before liquidation.

Computed here from Thorp's Eq. 7.13 (not stated in the sources): the chance of ever falling to 10% of starting capital (a 90% drawdown) is 10% at full Kelly, 0.1% at half Kelly, about 46% at 1.5x Kelly, and 100% at 2x Kelly or more. The chance of ever halving is about 79% at 1.5x Kelly. These are no-jump, continuous-rebalancing odds, so gaps make real odds worse (see the gap and jump claims).

Distance to liquidation shrinks roughly as 100% divided by leverage, before maintenance margin, fees and funding. Wealthsimple's table: 2x about 50%, 3x about 33%, 5x about 20%, 6x about 17%, 10x about 10%, 20x about 5%; actual liquidation comes sooner, and 'Halving your leverage roughly doubles the move it takes to liquidate you'. IG's illustrative table for a long: about 20% at 5x, 10% at 10x, 5% at 20x, 2% at 50x, with fees, funding and platform rules shifting the figures.

For an isolated linear (USDT- or USDC-margined) short, the documented formulas of Hyperliquid, dYdX and Binance all solve 'equity = maintenance margin, with maintenance margin measured at the liquidation price'. The result is LP = (margin + q × E) / (q × (1 + MMR)), where q is the position size, E is the entry price and MMR is the maintenance margin rate. If margin = q × E / L, this equals E × (1 + 1/L) / (1 + MMR). Hyperliquid writes liq_price = price − side × margin_available / position_size / (1 − l × side), with side = −1 for a short. dYdX writes p' = (e − s × p) / (|s| × MMF − s), with s

The 2025-10-10 event was predominantly a long-side liquidation cascade, not a short squeeze. Bitcoin.com (citing Bloomberg) reports more than $19B liquidated over about 24 hours, about $16.7B of it longs (data provider not named), with perp open interest down 43% from $217B to $123B and Hyperliquid's down 57% from $14B to $6B. Positioning beforehand was crowded long near record open interest. FTI adds elevated funding (about 10% to nearly 30% annualized by 2025-10-06) and notes funding and open interest had normalized or fallen more than 40% by December 2025.

Baseline carry for a perp short: the interest term is 0.01% per 8 hours (0.00125% per hour) on notional. That is about 10.95% a year simple, or 11.6% compounded. Hyperliquid's docs call it '11.6% APR paid to short', and Binance sets the same 0.01% per 8-hour interval for most symbols. The short earns this baseline only while the premium stays inside the clamp band. Outside the band, funding tracks the premium.

BitMEX's own study (press release dated 2025-10-14, 'The Anchor and the Ceiling') says funding was positive for over 92% of Q3 2025 across BitMEX, Binance and Hyperliquid. BitMEX BTC funding sat exactly on the 0.01% baseline for 78.19% of the quarter, and ETH for 87.52%. BitMEX argues large institutional inflows put a 'hard ceiling' on funding by shorting high-premium contracts. This is issuer-published, promotional content from a single source.

Estimator details in the main studies: Harvey et al. use the standard deviation of daily returns with exponentially decaying weights and a stated zero mean (20-day half-life in the headline exhibits, 90-day also tested), annualised, with exposure set from returns up to t-2 so the position is known 24 hours ahead, at a 10% annualised target. Moreira and Muir use the previous month's realized variance from daily returns. Both pick the scaling constant (k or c) ex post so scaled and unscaled series share the same full-sample volatility; Cederburg et al. note that c* is not known to an investor in

Tentative (derived, not stated by any source): at about 10x leverage the distance to liquidation is roughly 10% (100% divided by leverage, a little less after maintenance margin), the same size as Hyperliquid's 10% market TP/SL slippage tolerance. A stop-market order there is permitted to fill as far from its trigger as the whole liquidation distance. At 5x (about 20% away) the same tolerance leaves room.

The Bybit-style first-order formula and the closed form give different liquidation prices because they measure maintenance margin at different prices. The first-order form E × (1 + 1/L − MMR) uses maintenance margin at the entry price. The closed form E × (1 + 1/L)/(1 + MMR) uses maintenance margin at the liquidation price, which is higher for a short. The first-order cushion is therefore larger than the closed-form cushion by exactly the factor (1 + MMR) for a short, and smaller by the factor (1 − MMR) for a long. On dYdX's example inputs (9× effective leverage, MMR 5%) the first-order form g

Historically the short side has been paid on average, with large variation. He et al. find perpetual prices predominantly above their no-arbitrage value, with a standard deviation above twice the mean deviation for most tokens. BIS finds crypto futures carry averaging above 10% a year, larger than carry on equities, fixed income, currencies and commodities. BitMEX reports funding positive for over 92% of Q3 2025 across BitMEX, Binance and Hyperliquid.

JELLY, 2025-03-26: a trader's roughly $4M short on the JELLY perp ended up in Hyperliquid's HLP vault. Arkham (relayed by Cointelegraph) says the $4.1M short, opened within five minutes of $2.15M and $1.9M longs, was too large to liquidate immediately and was absorbed by HLP while JELLY rose 400%. CoinDesk and The Block put HLP's unrealized loss at $13.5M and about $12M. Validators voted to delist JELLY perps and force-settled positions at $0.0095 (CoinDesk). HYPE fell about 20-22%. Arkham says the whale made at least $6.26M.

Scale check (derived arithmetic, not a sourced finding): baseline funding of 0.01% per 8 hours is 0.03% of notional a day. A 10x short earns about 0.3% of its margin a day at that baseline. About 330 days of baseline carry therefore offset one 10% adverse price move, roughly the move that exhausts a 10x position's margin before maintenance margin is counted. Arkham's reported 400% JELLY price rise is far outside any funding offset.

Kelly sizing is hypersensitive to the estimated edge. MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba cite Chopra and Ziemba (1993): errors in means cost about 20 times as much as errors in covariances and 10 times as much as errors in variances (20:2:1). Gerlach et al. find their Kelly-type method 'most sensitive to errors in the expected return'. Thorp's worked case: if the true drift is half the estimate, betting the estimated Kelly gives zero growth (wild oscillation), betting 1.5x the estimated Kelly gives growth of -0.75 in units of m_e^2/(2 s^2) ('we will be ruined'), while betting half the estimated Kelly e

Shrink the Kelly fraction when the edge is uncertain. Thorp: assume the true edge is below the estimate (m_t < m_e) and choose f below the estimated Kelly by enough to keep growth above zero; f between 0.5 and 1.0 times the estimated Kelly protects against non-positive growth with 'a reduction of g that is likely to be no more than 25%'. His reasons: forecast excess returns are more likely too high than too low, prices are non-stationary, systems may be data-mined, and working systems attract capital that pushes returns down. Even with a real edge, Kelly sizing can lose most of the stake. MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba (citing Ziemba and Hausch): 700 wagers each with a 14% advantage can turn $1000 into $18 at full Kelly, while 16.6% of the time $1000 becomes at least $100,000; half Kelly can still leave $145 ('Half Kelly does not help much'). They list Long Term Capital as one of many real-world overbetting disasters. Gerlach et al., citing Ziemba (2016): however favourable the opportunities or long the horizon, a run of bad scenarios can cost most of the initial capital.

Computed here (accounting, not a finding from the cited page): a fixed-quantity position gains leverage as it loses. For a short opened at leverage L, after a price rise x equity is E0(1 - Lx) and notional is L E0 (1 + x), so leverage is L(1 + x)/(1 - Lx); at L = 5 a 10% rise lifts it to 11x. A long at the same L after a 10% fall reaches 9x, from L(1 - x)/(1 - Lx). Both blow up at x = 1/L, but the short's leverage climbs faster and its price has no cap.

Avellaneda and Zhang give an exact link for a daily-rebalanced fund with leverage ratio beta: its value is the underlying's value raised to the power beta, times exp(-(beta^2 - beta)/2 x realized variance), plus financing terms (funding rate, expense ratio, and 'the cost of borrowing shares in the case of short LETFs'). The holder is short realized variance 'irrespective of the sign of beta': the variance coefficient is 1 at beta = +2, 3 at beta = -2 and 3 at beta = +3. By the same formula (computed here) beta = -1 carries coefficient 1, equal to a 2x long fund, and beta = -3 carries 6, double

In the 10 October 2025 cascade, calm-market slippage assumptions failed. FTI Consulting (2025-12-24) reports that more than $19 billion of leverage was liquidated in roughly a day, BTC top-of-book depth fell by more than 90% on key venues, and bid-ask spreads widened from single-digit basis points to double-digit percentages at the extremes. CoinShares (2025-10-20) says large liquidity providers pulled liquidity, leaving order books dangerously thin, and cites Amberdata for futures open interest falling from $175 billion to $125 billion in under a day.

Carry is largest when leveraged long demand is strongest, and high carry has preceded crashes. BIS finds carry varies mainly with a convenience yield driven by trend-chasing, attention-driven leveraged long demand from smaller investors in booms and by scarce arbitrage capital. It finds high carry predicts future price crashes and rises alongside the price of crash insurance, with peaks up to 60% a year. FTI reports funding climbing from about 10% to nearly 30% annualized by 2025-10-06, four days before the 2025-10-10 liquidation. FTI's case is a single event, consistent with BIS but not an in

On crypto venues a spot short is the same borrow-and-sell trade, funded from a lending pool whose price moves with conditions. Kraken says funds from its BTC margin pool let a client short sell, charges the fee on the quantity of the asset sold (its BTC example: 'could be 0.010%'), locks the rollover rate at order execution and states that margin rates fluctuate with market conditions. Aave's variable borrow rate is a two-slope function of pool utilization, with a second slope applying from the optimal usage ratio to 100 percent utilization, set per reserve.

Observed multi-month results of daily-reset funds show the drag. FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-31 (2009-06-11): from 2008-12-01 to 2009-04-30 the Russell 1000 Financial Services Index gained about 8% while an ETF seeking 3x its daily return fell 53% and the ETF seeking 3x the inverse fell 90%; the Dow Jones U.S. Oil & Gas Index gained 2% while the 2x ETF fell 6% and the 2x inverse ETF fell 26%. Its two-day example: the index goes 100 to 101 to 100 and the inverse ETF loses 0.02%; it goes 100 to 110 to 100 and the inverse ETF loses 1.82% (checked here: 0.90 x 1.0909 - 1). FINRA: such ETFs 'typical

OKX does not publish a standalone futures liquidation price formula on the pages read. Its help page says position reduction or forced liquidation may be triggered when the maintenance margin ratio is at or below 100%, based on the mark price, and directs users to the built-in Futures Calculator (Liquidation Price tab). The calculator takes the pair, margin mode, direction, leverage, entry price, number of contracts and available margin.

Diagnostic for 'positive expected return but equity keeps shrinking': time-average growth is the arithmetic drift minus half the variance, g = mu - sigma^2/2 (MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba appendix: 'g_p = E_p - V_p/2' in continuous time). Peters' Figure 2 uses mu = 0.05 and sigma = 0.45 per time unit, giving g of about -0.051 (0.05 - 0.10125), with results noise-dominated until about 75 time units. At high volatility the volatility term dominates a modest edge even at 1x, before any leverage is added.

Crossing liquidation costs more than being stopped out. Hyperliquid: during backstop liquidation 'the maintenance margin is not returned to the user'. OKX: after forced liquidation it charges a liquidation fee on position value plus a deleveraging fee equal to the maintenance margin of the reduced position's tier, and under cross margin 'all margin allocated to the trading account may be lost'. dYdX v4 default settings: 'up to the entire remaining value of the account may be taken as penalty', though the engine 'will attempt to leave funds in accounts of positive value where possible' after a

Liquidation is not always all-or-nothing, which scopes the cost claim above. Hyperliquid sends liquidation orders to the book first and, for positions above 100k USDC, only 20% at a time (with a 30-second cooldown during which orders are for the entire position); if the maintenance margin requirement is met afterwards, 'any remaining collateral remains with the trader'. OKX describes a staged process of order cancellation, position reduction and forced liquidation, and stops reducing once the remaining position meets the new tier's requirement.

Carry is compressing. BitMEX (report press release, 2026-01-08) says funding-rate arbitrage became 'increasingly crowded' as exchange-native delta-neutral products grew, with yields falling toward 4% and often below US Treasury rates by mid-2025. He et al. find the annualized absolute deviation of perps from no-arbitrage prices fell about 22 percentage points a year, consistent with more arbitrage capital and competition, and that after 2022 futures-spot spreads are much closer to zero. They also find price convergence dominates arbitrage returns while funding payments play a minor and shrinki

Funding formula (Binance, mirrored by Hyperliquid): F = average premium index P + clamp(interest rate - P, -0.05%, +0.05%). The interest rate is 0.01% per 8-hour interval (0.03% a day) for most Binance symbols, and 0% for BNBUSDT and ETHBTC. Inside the clamp band, a premium between about -0.04% and +0.06% gives funding equal to the 0.01% interest rate. Binance announced on 2025-09-16 that from 2025-09-18 08:01 UTC it divides the result by 8/N, where N is the funding interval in hours. He et al. list the Binance parameters as kappa=1, gamma=0.05%, iota=0.01% and say Hyperliquid mirrors the spec

The only numeric stop-to-liquidation rule found is from Gainium (a trading-bot vendor; undated page, copyright 2026): 'Your leverage should place your liquidation price well below your stop loss — at least 2-3x further away', and 'Place it at least 20-30% of the distance before your liquidation price, not at it'. No exchange help page or regulator bulletin read for this concept gives a numeric ratio.

Binance funding intervals vary by contract and can shorten under stress. The announcement scales the formula by 8/N and gives a 4-hour PUMPUSDT example. FAQ section 8.1 (effective 2025-05-02) moves settlement from 8 or 4 hours to 1 hour after a settlement hits the cap or floor. Section 8.2 (effective 2026-01-02) returns it to 4 hours after 16 consecutive cycles with absolute funding at or below 0.025%. A short in a squeeze can therefore be charged more often.

Hyperliquid's docs, read 2026-11-06, say funding is capped at 0.5% per hour, 'much less aggressive capping than CEX counterparts', and that cap and interval do not depend on the asset. Hyperliquid's funding page is the only primary source read here, and a third-party guide dated 2026-06-11 gives a different cap (see disagreements).

The analyst heuristic that negative funding sets up a squeeze rests on very small samples. Cointelegraph (2025-07-03, CryptoQuant data) says negative funding in an uptrend 'often results in an overcrowded short trade vulnerable to a short squeeze' and cites only two earlier flips: September 2024 (about 80% gain) and July 2023 (about 150%). K33 via The Block (2026-04-15) says 46 consecutive days of negative 30-day average funding raise the likelihood of a short squeeze. It compares the streak with only two longer ones (March-May 2020, 63 days; June-August 2021, 49 days) and gives no outcome sta

Arithmetic expected wealth keeps rising with leverage while typical growth falls, so 'leverage destroys expected value' must be scoped. Peters: 'growth rates derived from ensemble-average returns depend linearly on leverage', which 'can thus incentivize investors to maximize leverage, which is detrimental to time-average growth and overall market stability'. MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba: under fairly general conditions maximizing expected log wealth also maximizes median log wealth, and bets above Kelly bring 'more risk and lower growth'. So leverage destroys expected log wealth, median wealth an

Leverage does not enter the fixed-fractional size; it only sets the margin needed. Kraken: 'Leverage doesn't change how much you should risk per trade.' Its worked examples: BTC-PERP long, $10,000 account, 1% risk, entry $60,000, stop $59,000 gives 0.1 BTC ($6,000 notional, $600 margin at 10x); ETH-PERP short, entry $3,200, stop $3,280 gives 1.25 ETH ($4,000 notional, $800 margin at 5x). The Tapeboard and Right Trader formulas also have no leverage term.

A correct perp short can still be force-closed by auto-deleveraging (ADL). When an account goes bankrupt and liquidators and the insurance fund cannot absorb it, venues close profitable opposite-side positions against it. Orderly: ADL fires only if liquidators do not take over, nobody claims the positions from the insurance fund, and the insurance fund margin ratio is below its minimum; it selects the traders with the most profit and the most leverage. Hyperliquid: opposite-side users are ranked by unrealized PnL and leverage and closed at the previous mark price against the underwater account

Funding-rate arbitrage (long spot, short perp), the capital that takes the other side of leveraged long demand, is not risk-free. He et al.: it 'is not risk-free even disregarding margin requirements and trading costs, simply because there is no predetermined expiration date when the trade would be unwound at a profit', and temporary worsening of apparent arbitrage opportunities 'can lead to liquidations and losses'. BIS: engaging in cash-and-carry is risky because of spikes in margins and liquidations amid drawdowns.

Overbetting past 2x Kelly destroys growth. In continuous time, betting exactly twice the Kelly amount gives a growth rate equal to the risk-free rate (zero excess growth); beyond 2x, growth is below the risk-free rate and eventually negative. With r = 0 the growth relative to the maximum at c x Kelly is c(2 - c): 0.5x and 1.5x both give 75%, 2x gives 0. MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba Table 3 (blackjack, 2% edge) shows 2x Kelly with relative growth 0.00 and a 0.50 chance of doubling before halving. Carver reaches the same result: doubling the optimal leverage 'results in the geometric mean falling t

De-risk as drawdown grows. MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba: practitioners who wish to protect capital above all 'sharply reduce risk as their drawdown increases'. The original Turtle rules, as reproduced on a blog, cut the notional account by 20% for each 10% drawdown, so position size shrank faster than equity.

The liquidation price a venue displays is an estimate and can move. Hyperliquid: the figure shown while entering a trade can differ because book liquidity changes, and after opening it can still differ because of funding payments or changes in unrealized PnL of other cross positions. OKX: 'the estimated liquidation price is not the actual price at which liquidation will occur', and in USDT cross-margin mode it cannot be calculated when the account holds two or more USDT futures or leveraged positions in different pairs. KuCoin: in cross margin, positions are liquidated only when the risk ratio

Continuous-time Kelly for one risky asset with drift m, volatility s and risk-free rate r: f* = (m - r)/s^2, growth g(f) = r + f(m - r) - s^2 f^2 / 2 (an exact parabola in f), and maximum growth g(f*) = r + (m - r)^2 / (2 s^2) = r + S^2/2, where S is the Sharpe ratio. The fraction f is a multiple of equity, so f above 1 is leverage. Because f* x s = S, the Kelly-consistent annualised volatility target equals the Sharpe ratio.

Evidence for the benefit and its scope. Harvey et al. (five of six authors work at Man AHL or Man Group, the sixth advises Man Group; 60+ assets, daily data from 1926): US equity Sharpe ratio rises from 0.40 to 0.48-0.51 over 1927-2017 at a 10% volatility target; the gain is confined to risk assets (equities, credit) and portfolios holding many of them; for bonds, currencies and commodities the Sharpe effect is negligible. They tie the gain to the leverage effect (volatility rises when prices fall), which makes scaling momentum-like. Moreira and Muir report for the market portfolio an alpha of

ADL candidate ranking is venue-specific, so check the venue's docs before assuming who gets cut. Orderly ranks by profit and leverage; Hyperliquid sorts by (mark_price / entry_price) * (notional_position / account_value); Campbell et al. show that for single-asset isolated margin, reducing the highest-leverage accounts first (a 'minimax leverage' water-filling rule) is optimal for all monotone risk measures.

A short position is a negative Kelly fraction. Thorp: in the continuous model f < 0 'simply corresponds to selling the security short. If m < r this could be advantageous', so Kelly shorts only when the expected return is below the risk-free rate. Gerlach et al. use the same convention: their invested fraction lambda is limited to [-1, 2] in practice (at most 200% long or 100% short).

Carver's translation of Kelly into a volatility target: with Gaussian returns the full-Kelly annualised risk target equals the expected Sharpe ratio (expected SR 0.5 means 50% annualised risk). He calls half Kelly 'a far safer bet', cut his own target to 25% a year ('closer to the 10 - 20% that most systematic trend following firms target'), and halves backtested performance as a rule of thumb because most backtests are overfitted. Thorp's identity f* x s = S gives the same result.

Computed here from g(L): with constant leverage the variance drag is L^2 sigma^2 / 2 a year, and the break-even excess return (zero log growth) is L sigma^2 / 2. At 60% volatility, 2x needs 36% a year, 5x needs 90% and 10x needs 180%; at 30% volatility the figures are 9%, 22.5% and 45%. The drag alone at 60% volatility is 72% a year of log growth at 2x and 450% at 5x. For a short the edge term flips sign: g_short(L) - r = -L(mu - r) - L^2 sigma^2 / 2 before borrow and funding costs. With a positive risk premium both terms are negative and no short leverage breaks even; a short only pays when e

Do not state the drag as a certain loss; it scales with realized variance and depends on trend. Avellaneda and Zhang: leveraged ETFs 'outperform the static leveraged strategy only when return are large and volatility is small' (their wording), there are 'a few periods where LETFs outperform', and with dynamic rebalancing, about weekly in their sample, a leveraged fund can replicate the index multiple. Forsyth, van Staden and Li (2025 preprint abstract): leveraged ETFs remain poorly suited to passive or static approaches, yet simple dynamic strategies that cut risk after gains can use the compo

A short has no loss ceiling; a long cannot lose more than it paid. Binance Academy (updated 2026-07-06): 'The most significant risk of a short position is that losses are theoretically unlimited', while for a long 'the worst case is losing your entire investment'; it adds that a short 'can result in losses that exceed the initial collateral'. Wikipedia: 'the potential losses of a short-seller are also theoretically unlimited', and a broker may cover a short 'immediately and without their consent' when the price skyrockets. With leverage L the short's equity is gone after a rise of about 1/L an

Bybit's isolated-margin formula, as transcribed in the freqtrade docstring that cites Bybit's help center, is: Short USDT liquidation price = Entry Price + (Initial Margin − Maintenance Margin) / Contract Quantity + Extra Margin Added / Contract Quantity (for a long, subtract both terms). freqtrade implements it with initial margin = notional / leverage and maintenance margin = notional × MMR, both at the entry price, ignores extra margin, and raises an error for inverse contracts. With no extra margin this equals E × (1 + 1/L − MMR).

Tail effects: Harvey et al. find volatility targeting 'consistently reduces the likelihood of extreme returns (and the volatility of volatility)' across 60+ assets, cutting both left and right tails, and lowers maximum drawdowns for the 60/40 and risk-parity portfolios. Moreira and Muir report that their strategy worked in the Great Depression, 1987 and 2008 and, per their appendix, does not create fatter left tails than the original factors.

Constant-leverage growth is a downward parabola in leverage. In continuous time, holding leverage L on an asset with drift mu, volatility sigma and risk-free rate r gives time-average growth g(L) = r + L(mu - r) - L^2 sigma^2 / 2. Peters: the positive contribution 'is linear in the leverage, but the negative contribution is quadratic', so g/L^2 tends to -sigma^2/2 as L grows, and growth peaks at L* = (mu - r)/sigma^2. MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba: for processes close to continuous time, growth 'becomes zero plus the risk free rate when one bets exactly twice the Kelly wager', and beyond that it t

ADL has actually fired on a major venue. Hyperliquid's cross-margin ADL triggered during the October 10, 2025 event, reported as its first cross-margin ADL in over two years (WuBlockchain, 27 November 2025), and Campbell et al. use that event as their case study, reporting that their risk-minimizing allocations achieve lower expected shortfall than the exchange's realized allocation.

Ruin is not capped at the deposit. FXCM said on 2015-01-15 that clients' losses after the Swiss National Bank announcement 'generated negative equity balances owed to FXCM of approximately $225 million' and that it 'may be in breach of some regulatory capital requirements'. On 2015-01-28 CNBC reported that FXCM would forgive about 90% of clients with negative balances in certain jurisdictions. Binance Academy says a short 'can result in losses that exceed the initial collateral'. ESMA's negative balance protection answers the same gap risk. Both FXCM items trace to FXCM's own statements.

It takes very long to verify an edge. MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba (citing Thorp 2006): in a continuous-time model with drifts of 20% and 10% and equal 10% volatility, five years gives 95% confidence that the higher-drift strategy leads; if the better strategy has 20% volatility against 10%, it takes 157 years. Inference, not stated by the source: edge-dependent sizing rests on inputs a trader cannot confirm within a realistic horizon.

Worked relation between fixed-fractional risk and Kelly (computed here): for a binary-payoff trade the Kelly wager is edge divided by odds (MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba). A system that wins 40% of trades at +2R and loses 60% at -1R has an edge of 0.2R per trade and Kelly f* = 0.1, i.e. 10% of equity at risk per trade, so a 1-2% fixed-fractional rule is 0.1-0.2x Kelly. If the true win rate is 33.3% the edge is zero. Kraken presents a fixed 0.5-2% approach as more practical than Kelly for traders without a large trade history.

A stop price is a trigger, not a guaranteed fill. SEC staff (equities): a stop order becomes a market order at the stop price, and its execution price 'can deviate significantly from the stop price due to the prices of available liquidity'; a stop-limit 'may not be executed if the stock's price moves away from the specified limit price'. The same failure shows on perps: Hyperliquid's FAQ says a long stop-loss with a $10 limit 'may rest at $10 without filling' if price drops from $11 to $9, and Mudrex says a skipped stop-limit can leave the position to be liquidated.

Two regulators measured heavy retail losses on leveraged CFDs and answered by limiting leverage. ESMA (2018-03-27): national authority analyses found '74-89% of retail accounts typically lose money', with average losses of EUR 1,600 to EUR 29,000 per client; its measures cap leverage from 30:1 (major currency pairs) through 20:1, 10:1 and 5:1 (single equities) to 2:1 (cryptocurrencies), and add a 50% margin close-out rule and negative balance protection, 'an overall guaranteed limit on retail client losses'. FCA (2016-12-06): its analysis found '82% of clients lost money', some retail leverage

Selling before shares are delivered is not itself unlawful: the SEC says 'naked' short selling 'is not necessarily a violation' of the securities laws or its rules. The hard edge is the close-out in Rule 204: a fail to deliver from a short sale must be closed out by purchasing or borrowing like securities by the start of regular trading hours on the settlement day following the settlement date (third consecutive settlement day for long-sale fails). A participant that misses the deadline, and brokers that route orders to it, may take no short sale in that security without first borrowing it (pr

Pick the stop first, size from it, and treat leverage as an output. Kraken's sizing guide uses position size = (account value x risk %) / |entry - stop|, identical for shorts (stop above entry); leverage 'doesn't change the dollar risk if the stop is hit', and 'Never let your leverage setting determine how large a position you open'. Wealthsimple: 'The maximum leverage a platform allows is a limit, not a recommendation.'

Squeeze-watching inputs in the cited analyses: CryptoQuant funding charts (7-day moving average) and CoinGlass liquidation estimates (Cointelegraph), and Skew, Laevitas, Coinglass, Bybit, Binance and BitMEX data (K33). K33 cautioned in 2022 that Binance and Bybit had reduced liquidation data access, so Coinglass figures understate liquidations. That caveat is from one source, dated 2022-09-27, and may be out of date.

Borrow-and-sell carry is quoted as a loan fee or as a rebate rate on the cash collateral. The SEC says the short seller pays interest on the loan and passes dividends to the lender. D'Avolio defines extreme specials as stocks 'demanding negative rebate rates (i.e., loan fees in excess of the risk-free rate)', and the 2025 paper's Table 1 pairs each fee with a rebate that mirrors it, for example ARMP at a 1000 percent fee and a -994.83 percent rebate.

Inference, not tested in the sources: because BIS ties high carry to trend-chasing leveraged long demand in booms, and FTI shows funding rising into the pre-crash rally, a naked perp short collects the most funding in the phase when price momentum against it is strongest. Funding is then a risk premium for squeeze and rally risk, not free yield.

ECB Financial Stability Review box (May 2020; the page gives only the month): a stylised four-asset risk-parity portfolio would have had to sell assets worth nearly 225% of its capital to meet its volatility target in March 2020, leaving a cash share near 25%. Estimates of money in volatility strategies run up to USD 2 trillion, including about USD 300 billion in some 100 risk-parity funds. The ECB says the model figures are not observed data and the contribution of these strategies to price moves 'remains hard to quantify'.

Fixed-fractional sizing: choose the fraction of current equity to lose if the stop is hit, then size = equity x risk% / |entry - stop|. Kraken, Tapeboard and The Right Trader give this formula. Because the base is current equity, dollar risk grows with the account and shrinks after losses. Kraken: 'A common approach is to risk 0.5% to 2% of account per trade'; The Right Trader: the fraction is 'something you choose' and 'not a forecast', and 1% is 'a common retail choice, not a law'.

Turtle volatility-normalised unit sizing: N is a 20-day exponential average of true range (a precursor of ATR); dollar volatility = N x dollars per point; 'Units were sized so that 1 N represented 1% of the account equity'; limits include four units per market and 12 units in one direction. This is fixed-fractional risk with ATR-normalised size, so it shrinks positions when volatility rises, as volatility targeting does.

The bankruptcy price is the price at which a position's equity reaches zero, and for a short it lies above the liquidation price. KuCoin defines Bankruptcy Value = Position Mark Value − |Position Mark Value| × Total Position AMR and, for USDT-margined contracts, Bankruptcy Price = Bankruptcy Value ÷ Position Quantity. For one isolated short at inception this gives E × (1 + 1/L), against a liquidation price of E × (1 + 1/L)/(1 + m): a 50× short at 30,000 USDT has bankruptcy price 30,600 and liquidation price 30,459.9 at m = 0.46% (computed). KuCoin places its risk-reduction IOC orders at the ba

The liquidation price marks where a venue starts reducing a position, not necessarily where the position closes. KuCoin (isolated): it cancels open orders, steps the position down one risk tier, and cuts size with IOC orders at the bankruptcy price until the margin ratio recovers, taking the whole position only at the lowest tier. Hyperliquid: for a liquidatable position above 100k USDC only 20% is sent to the book, followed by a 30-second cooldown; if the book fills the order, remaining collateral stays with the trader, but a backstop liquidation (equity below 2/3 of maintenance margin) trans

Binance Futures lets the trader pick Last Price or Mark Price as the stop trigger. Its stop-order FAQ (updated 2026-03-11) says the trigger for a stop-limit order is 'Last Price' by default and the trigger for a stop-market order is 'Mark Price' by default. A stop-limit left on its default is therefore keyed to a different price than the one that triggers liquidation, while the Binance blog calls Mark Price triggers 'a better option for avoiding liquidation'.

Two-stop pattern: Binance suggests one Last Price-triggered stop to limit excessive losses and a separate Mark Price-triggered stop to help avoid liquidation. Mudrex likewise advises matching the stop trigger to Mark Price and keeping a 'safety distance' from liquidation.

Binance's blog says Price Protection can stop a stop order from firing: when Last Price and Mark Price exceed a predetermined threshold the function 'will prevent the stop order from being triggered, thereby causing the order to expire', and a stop-limit can expire if its limit price is unavailable in the order book. The Binance Futures stop-order FAQ (updated 2026-03-11) does not mention Price Protection, so current behaviour is unconfirmed.

Lower leverage is the main lever on the buffer. IG: 'Many risk frameworks suggest 3x to 5x as a starting point' (liquidation roughly 33% to 20% from entry on the 100%-divided-by-leverage rule). Wealthsimple: 'The most reliable way to avoid it is to use less leverage than you're permitted.'

A stock lender can end the loan at any time (a recall), which is the borrow-side forced-exit path. D'Avolio found recalls rare in 2000-2001 (about 2 percent of stocks on loan per average month) but slow to repair: a recalled short seller needed a mean of 23 (median 9) trading days to re-establish the loan, and days on which recalled borrowers might be forced to cover show extraordinary volume and intraday volatility. If no replacement lender is found, any resulting fail is subject to the Rule 204 close-out deadline (a link this note infers from the two sources).

At the same leverage L and maintenance rate m, the closed-form cushion between entry and liquidation, as a fraction of the entry price, is (1/L − m)/(1 + m) for a short and (1/L − m)/(1 − m) for a long, so a short always has the smaller percentage cushion. At m = 0.5% the short cushions are about 49.3% at 2×, 19.4% at 5×, 9.45% at 10×, 4.48% at 20×, 1.49% at 50× and 0.50% at 100× (computed from the formula). At 1× a linear long cannot be liquidated (its liquidation price tends to 0), but a linear short at 1× is liquidated near 2E / (1 + m), roughly when the price doubles, because a short's los

Stops reduce expected return unless returns have momentum, so a stop is risk control, not a return source. Kaminski and Lo (SIFR 2008 abstract): 'under the Random Walk Hypothesis, simple 0/1 stop-loss rules always decrease a strategy's expected return', but 'in the presence of momentum, stop-loss rules can add value'. The 2014 Journal of Financial Markets abstract says that at longer sampling frequencies certain stop-loss policies on daily index-futures data can increase expected return while substantially reducing volatility. The abstracts do not mention leverage or liquidation.

Hyperliquid's default slippage tolerance for market TP/SL orders is 10%. The limit price on a TP/SL order sets the slippage bound instead: a more aggressive limit makes a fill more likely but allows more slippage. In the docs' example, a long stop-loss triggered at $10 with a $10 limit may rest unfilled if price gaps down, while an $8 limit would likely fill between $9 and $8.

Venue stress can remove the manual escape hatch. FTI says 'frozen exchange interfaces' prevented some traders from managing risk dynamically. CoinShares reports Lighter acknowledged a severe outage between 22:30 and 03:00 EST, dYdX was offline almost eight hours, and Binance cited systems under high load and intermittent delays. Binance's own statement says some platform modules had brief technical failures after 21:18 UTC while its 'core futures and spot matching engines and API trading functions all maintained normal operations'.

For a short, the protective stop is a buy-stop above entry. SEC staff: 'A buy stop order is entered at a stop price above the current market price' and is generally used 'to limit a loss or to protect a profit on a stock that they have sold short'. Kraken: 'For shorts, the stop-loss is above the entry price.'

Leverage versus edge (computed here from f* = (m - r)/s^2): holding leverage L at the Kelly optimum for an asset with 60% annualised volatility needs an expected net excess return of L x 0.36 per year: 108% for 3x, 360% for 10x, 720% for 20x. Thorp's S&P 500 inputs (excess return 5%, volatility 15%) give Kelly leverage 2.22; the same 5% excess return at 60% volatility gives about 0.14. For a short, the figure to compare is the expected return of the short after funding and borrow costs.

Compare the two shorts on five axes so failure modes stay distinct (synthesis of the claims above): access gate (locate and lender supply vs margin only); carry (loan fee or rebate vs signed funding, plus a borrow fee on pool-based perps); forced-exit path (recall and Rule 204 close-out vs liquidation and ADL); leverage ceiling (Reg T and FINRA 4210 vs venue tiers); price exposure (the asset itself vs the perp, which has basis).

Funding is charged on current notional, so a squeeze raises the dollar funding bill on a short even at an unchanged rate. Binance: Funding Amount = Nominal Value of Positions x Funding Rate, with nominal value at mark price. Hyperliquid: payment = position size x spot oracle price x funding rate, using the spot oracle rather than the mark price. If price doubles, the dollar funding per unit of size doubles.

Overbetting is worse than underbetting. 1.5x Kelly has the same relative growth as 0.5x Kelly (75%) but a lower chance of doubling before halving (0.56 versus 0.89 in MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba Table 3), so risk rises while growth falls. Thorp: because 'overbetting' is much more harmful than underbetting, fractional Kelly is prudent to the extent the inputs are uncertain. Carver: 'using less than the optimal leverage doesn't hurt much, using more hurts a lot'.

Fixed-fractional risk is capped only if the stop fills. Tapeboard: 'The formula assumes the stop fills at the stop price' and 'Gaps, halts, and slippage can make the realized loss exceed the budget'. The Right Trader: 'The fraction caps a stop that fills. It does not cap a gap or a liquidation that sits closer than the stop.' Thorp's 23% one-day S&P 500 drop in October 1987 shows the size gaps can reach. (Stop versus liquidation placement belongs to a sibling concept.)

Funding payments consume margin and can move liquidation closer. Binance debits funding from the futures available balance first and then from position margin, which can affect the liquidation price. Hyperliquid warns the displayed liquidation price may differ from the actual one because of funding payments and unrealized PnL in other positions.

Fee treatment differs by venue, so a generic formula is off by the fee term. KuCoin's isolated formula puts the liquidation fee rate (LFR) beside the maintenance rate in the denominator: for a USDT-margined short it is (1 + MMR + LFR). OKX's published maintenance-margin-ratio formulas divide by (MMR + fees), and its liquidation fee is charged on position value rather than margin. Hyperliquid states that there is no clearance fee on liquidations. Binance's variable list has no fee term, and freqtrade does not model liquidation fees. Example: a 50× short at 30,000 USDT with MMR 0.4% liquidates a

A perp short pays or receives signed funding rather than a loan fee. When the perp trades above the index price, funding is positive and longs pay shorts; when it trades below, shorts pay longs. Hyperliquid also builds in a fixed interest component of 0.01 percent per 8 hours (11.6 percent APR) paid to shorts, described as the difference in cost to borrow USD versus spot crypto; He et al. likewise note that when perp and spot are close the funding rate is fixed at a small positive value.

Liquidation is evaluated on mark price, not last traded price, on the venues checked. Binance says mark price 'always coincides with the liquidation price of a futures contract' and that a last-price trigger is 'not a foolproof method to avoid liquidation since the liquidation price is always the Mark Price'. Hyperliquid says 'Liquidations use the mark price'. OKX says the liquidation price 'is based on the mark price, rather than the last price or the index price'. IG says 'it is the mark price — not the last traded price — that triggers liquidation'.

Negative funding is not by itself a squeeze signal. K33 (2022-09-27) judged a rally after months of mostly negative funding as 'not fueled by shorts getting squeezed but rather more longs entering the market': BTC short liquidations were about $26M, in line with recent averages, while BTC open interest hit a record 424,000 BTC, and negative funding reflected few traders willing to add long exposure. Cointelegraph (2026-04-16) read funding that stayed negative while BTC rebounded above $75,000 as 'losses from bears rather than conviction' and weak bullish leverage demand, not as a squeeze setup

Cascade precursors are event-specific. Garcia Seuma (arXiv 2607.27070, 2026-07-29, single-author preprint, abstract-level read) studied seven BTC liquidation cascades from 2022 to 2025, including 2025-10-10. 'No variable is event-invariant.' Price showed critical slowing down in five of seven events and not in the two tariff-news shocks. In October 2025 the signal appeared in leverage rather than price, in-sample. Only compression of taker order-flow variance held across all events with data, as a population-level precursor (Fisher-combined p about 5e-6 on a 300-onset placebo test), not a per-

K33 (2022-09-27) reports BitMEX perps accumulated about -1.46% of funding in the roughly 318 days since the 2021 peak, so a persistent short would have paid about 1.46% in total. The same point in the 2018 bear market was -0.46%, and the May 2019 trough was -12.15%. BitMEX then held about 3.3% of perp open interest versus over 50% in 2018, so the comparison is not like-for-like.

A perp short carries basis risk that a borrow-and-sell short does not, because it is short the contract rather than the asset. He et al.: perpetuals 'are not guaranteed to converge to the spot price', and deviations from no-arbitrage prices in crypto are larger than in traditional currency markets (though they diminish over time). BIS researchers find 'excess volatility' of crypto futures relative to spot prices (a futures-wide finding, not perp-specific).

Liquidation triggers on a venue-defined reference price, not the last traded price. OKX: the liquidation price is based on the mark price, 'rather than the last price or the index price'. Hyperliquid: liquidations use a mark price that combines external CEX prices with Hyperliquid's book state. KuCoin: an isolated position enters liquidation when the mark price reaches the estimated liquidation price. dYdX: account value is estimated with the oracle price.

Backtests and bull-market samples overstate the edge. Carver: 'most back tests are overfitted'; 'Overestimating the Sharpe ratio of a negative skew asset and Kelly betting accordingly is a one way ticket to bankruptcy'; in his 2016 post negative skew reduces the optimal leverage and standard deviation target. Thorp notes the Kelly inputs in his case study came from 1982-1997, 'the greatest bull market in history', so the means were likely overestimates.

A perp short swaps lender-side forced exits for venue-side ones; it does not remove forced exit. On Hyperliquid, equity below maintenance margin first sends market orders to the book; below two-thirds of maintenance margin without a successful liquidation, a liquidator vault takes the position and the maintenance margin is not returned; ADL is the final backstop. A borrow-and-sell short instead faces recall and the Rule 204 close-out.

Kelly sizing maximizes the expected log of wealth, which maximizes the limiting exponential growth rate of wealth. Thorp's Theorem 1: if the per-bet growth rate g(f) is above zero, wealth tends to infinity almost surely; if g(f) is below zero, wealth tends to zero almost surely (ruin is almost sure); at g(f) = 0 wealth oscillates between 0 and infinity. MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba name the main drawback: the suggested wagers can be very large, so Kelly is very risky in the short term.

Auto-deleveraging (ADL) can close winning shorts. Hyperliquid: if an account's value or isolated position value goes negative, opposite-side users are ranked by unrealized PnL and leverage using (mark_price / entry_price) x (notional_position / account_value), and are closed at the previous mark price. FTI: on 2025-10-10 'some of the best-hedged shorts found their positions reduced or entirely closed', which can turn a hedged portfolio into a naked one. BitMEX: ADL across multiple exchanges disrupted delta-neutral strategies, forced professional market makers to cut liquidity, and left order b

Maintenance margin is tiered by position notional, and the tier terms enter the liquidation price. Binance: Maintenance Margin = Notional × Rate − Amount, and the maintenance amount (cumB, cumL or cumS) is a term in the liquidation formula. Hyperliquid: maintenance_margin = notional_position_value × maintenance_margin_rate − maintenance_deduction, where the deduction keeps total maintenance margin continuous in position size, and the liquidation formula uses the tier that matches the position value at the liquidation price.

The liquidation level moves, so a stop placed once against the displayed liquidation price can go stale. Hyperliquid: the shown price 'still may not be the actual liquidation price due to funding payments or changes in unrealized pnl in other positions (for cross margin positions)'. OKX: the estimate 'is not the actual price at which liquidation will occur'. Binance: 'The liquidation price can change and the stop-loss order may not protect positions from liquidation'. Wealthsimple: fees and funding shrink the buffer further.

The JELLY squeeze ran on thin spot liquidity, and the venue resolved it by discretion. CoinDesk says DEX liquidity was minimal, so moving the price was relatively easy, and that oracles took the DEX price. Validators froze and force-settled the market, and the Hyper Foundation said users other than flagged addresses would be compensated. Binance and OKX listed JELLY perps within about an hour while Hyperliquid halted (The Block). Commentary relayed by Cointelegraph said the intervention raised decentralization questions. None of the three articles mentions funding rates.

Every venue encodes 'short' through a sign, and a wrong sign puts a short's liquidation price below its entry price. Binance: Side = 1 for long and −1 for short. Hyperliquid: side = 1 for long and −1 for short. dYdX: the position size s is negative for a short. KuCoin: side = −1 for a short, and its cross-margin section states that USDT-margined short quantities and values are negative, while coin-margined short quantities and values are positive. A short's liquidation price must come out above its entry price; use that as a sanity check.

Design lag: volatility targeting sizes from past data, so a one-day gap hits the pre-shock exposure. Harvey et al. set exposure from returns up to t-2, Moreira and Muir from the previous month's variance, and Thorp's Kelly results require 'instantaneous' adjustment. This follows from the designs; none of the sources tests a single-day shock against a volatility-targeted position.

Cross margin changes the equity term: the liquidation price depends on the whole account. Binance: in cross mode WB is the cross wallet balance and the formula subtracts the maintenance margin of all other contracts (TMM1) and adds their unrealized PnL (UPNL1); in isolated mode TMM = 0, UPNL = 0 and WB is the isolated wallet balance. dYdX: the cross formula p' = (e − s × p − MMR_o) / (|s| × MMF − s) subtracts MMR_o, the maintenance requirement of the other positions. Hyperliquid: margin_available is account_value − maintenance_margin_required for cross and isolated_margin − maintenance_margin_

A workable recipe for a short's liquidation price on a linear perpetual: (1) take equity: the margin for isolated, or account value minus other positions' maintenance margin plus their unrealized PnL for cross. (2) Take the maintenance rate m and maintenance amount for the tier that applies at the liquidation price. (3) Solve equity + q × (E − P) = m × q × P − amount for P, giving P = (equity + q × E + amount) / (q × (1 + m)). (4) Add venue fee terms, such as KuCoin's liquidation fee rate, to m. (5) If P falls in a different tier, redo steps 2 and 3. (6) Compare with the venue's displayed figu

A borrow-and-sell short in US equities starts with a loan. The SEC describes a short sale as a sale of stock the seller does not own or will borrow for delivery: the seller's brokerage typically lends the shares (from firm inventory, other clients' margin accounts or another lender), the short seller pays interest on the loan and must pass along any dividends the stock pays. D'Avolio opens from the same premise: to short a stock an arbitrageur must first borrow it.

Sign convention: if the perpetual trades above the spot index, funding is positive and longs pay shorts. If it trades below, funding is negative and shorts pay longs. Binance's FAQ, Hyperliquid's docs and He, Manela, Ross and von Wachter all state this.

Settlement timing differs by venue. Binance's default interval is every 8 hours at 00:00, 08:00 and 16:00 UTC, with a 15-second tolerance, and a trader pays or receives only if the position is open at the funding time, so closing earlier avoids that payment. Hyperliquid settles every hour at one eighth of the computed 8-hour rate.

Most US stocks are cheap to borrow, but the price of borrowing has a fat tail. D'Avolio's April 2000 to September 2001 data: 91 percent of stocks on loan cost under 1 percent a year (value-weighted mean 17 basis points, 'general collateral'), about 9 percent were 'specials' averaging 4.3 percent a year, and fewer than 1 percent were extreme specials with negative rebates. Daniel, Klos and Rottke find 68 percent of 2024:01-2025:06 stock-day observations under 1 percent a year (a different base from D'Avolio's, so not like-for-like).

The hard-to-borrow tail has grown, per one preliminary 2025 paper. The share of US stocks with a borrow cost above 1 percent a year rose from about 10 percent in June 2003 to 43 percent in July 2022; the share above 10 percent went from a handful of issues in 2003 to just under 20 percent in August 2023; 2024:01-2025:06 had 42,978 stock-day observations above 100 percent a year (over 113 stocks a day), with ARMP at 1000 percent annualized. A high-borrow-cost portfolio's ex-post borrow cost (about 84.8 percent) exceeded its 81.4 percent gross short alpha.

Shorting spot crypto was a binding constraint early on. He et al. state that in the early years of their sample 'the infrastructure for shorting cryptocurrencies was underdeveloped', and the trade for a perp below spot requires shorting spot and investing the proceeds in the cash market, so they also test a long-spot-only variant. The Kraken page shows pool-funded shorts now exist, but pool depth for small tokens was not measured.

Funding turns negative in crash and bear regimes, and shorts then pay. He et al. show the FTX collapse (November 2022) produced significantly negative funding on all solvent exchanges, with perp prices below spot. K33 reports funding was mostly negative from the June 2022 credit crisis and neutral to below neutral since 2021-12-04.

Inference from the tier rules: a short's notional rises as the price rises, so a large short can move into a higher-rate tier before it reaches the liquidation price that a flat-rate formula gives. A long's notional falls as its price falls, so the same tier effect works in its favour. Hyperliquid solves for the tier at the liquidation price; a flat-rate calculator does not, and so can overstate a large short's cushion.

Open question: Scope check on the leverage-effect mechanism for crypto: Harvey et al. tie the Sharpe gain from volatility targeting to the equity leverage effect and did not test crypto. Baur and Dimpfl (Economics Letters 2018) report, for the 20 largest cryptocurrencies, that positive shocks raise volatility more than negative shocks, the opposite of equities. Kakinaka and Umeno (Physica A 2021, a different method) find price-volatility cross-correlations stronger in downtrends for BTC and ETH but inverted for XRP and LTC. Only the abstracts of the two crypto papers were read.
facts.note: crypto leverage effect untested by Harvey et al.; two crypto papers disagree on sign (abstract-level read)

facts.text: Controversy: Real-time value is contested. Cederburg, O'Doherty, Wang and Yan (JFE 2020) test 103 equity strategies: volatility-managed versions beat unmanaged ones on Sharpe ratio in 53 cases and lost in 50, with only 8 significant wins (mostly momentum-related). Moreira-Muir-style spanning alphas hold in-sample but rely on combining scaled and unscaled portfolios with ex post optimal weights; realistic out-of-sample combinations earned a lower certainty-equivalent return than the unmanaged portfolio in 72 of 103 cases (market: Sharpe 0.42 versus 0.46), which the authors attribute to structural instabilit
facts.note: Cederburg et al. vs Moreira-Muir/Harvey et al. on out-of-sample value of volatility targeting

facts.text: Controversy: Why volatility targeting can work: volatility clusters and is forecastable, while average returns show no clear pattern across buckets of lagged volatility, so return per unit of risk is lower after high-volatility periods. Moreira and Muir: variance is highly forecastable at short horizons and variance forecasts are only weakly related to future returns. Harvey et al.: expected returns 'do not seem to reflect the persistence in volatility'. Inference: this sizes off the better-estimated input (variance) instead of the worse one (the mean), the reverse of Kelly's dependence on the drift.

Controversy: Volatility targeting sets exposure inversely to forecast volatility, so portfolio risk stays constant rather than notional exposure: leverage up when volatility is low, down when it is high. Moreira and Muir scale monthly returns by c divided by the previous month's realized variance (inverse-variance scaling); Harvey et al. scale by sigma_target divided by a volatility estimate known 24 hours ahead (inverse-volatility scaling), which they note has lower turnover than variance scaling.
